results.question: According to “A new clump-based star formation model for galaxy simulations: implications for high-redshift compact star clusters”, how do changes in disc compactness between the z = 0 and z = 10 setups of 10^10 M☉ haloes affect (a) the maximum gas clump mass and surface density, (b) the fraction of clumps exceeding a surface density threshold Σc,th = 300 M☉ pc^-2, and (c) the global star formation efficiency at t = 3 t_dyn? Please answer with the quantitative values reported in the paper.
results.reference_answer:
(a) Maximum clump mass increases from ≈ 10^5.1 M☉ at z = 0 to ≈ 10^7.4 M☉ at z = 10; maximum clump surface density increases from ≈ 10^2.9 M☉ pc^-2 to > 10^4.0 M☉ pc^-2. (evidence_id: 0c3dbf13da9dd4027969933c)

(b) The fraction of clumps with Σc ≥ 300 M☉ pc^-2 rises from 0.25 at z = 0 to 0.34 at z = 6 and 0.38 at z = 10. (evidence_id: 0c3dbf13da9dd4027969933c)

(c) The global star formation efficiency at t = 3 t_dyn increases monotonically from 5 × 10^-3 at z = 0 to 2 × 10^-1 at z = 10 (for the 10^10 M☉ haloes). (evidence_id: 160dd9270d4a618cf6df643a)
results.answer:
The maximum gas clump mass increases from approximately 10^5.1 M⊙ at z=0 to approximately 10^7.4 M⊙ at z=10 in 10^10 M⊙ haloes. [1] [2]

The maximum gas clump surface density increases from approximately 10^2.3 M⊙ pc^-2 at z=0 to greater than 10^4.0 M⊙ pc^-2 at z=10 in 10^10 M⊙ haloes. [1] [2]

The fraction of gas clumps exceeding the surface density threshold of 300 M⊙ pc^-2 rises from approximately 0.25 (25%) at z=0 to 0.38 (38%) at z=10 in 10^10 M⊙ haloes. [1] [2]

The global star formation efficiency at t = 3 t_dyn increases from approximately 5 × 10^-3 (0.005) at z=0 to approximately 2 × 10^-1 (0.2) at z=10 in 10^10 M⊙ haloes. [1]

Applying this model to isolated disc galaxies embedded in haloes of _𝑀_ h = 10[9] , 10[10] and 10[[11]] M⊙, with disc compactness corresponding to redshift⊙, with disc compactness corresponding to redshift, with disc compactness corresponding to redshift _𝑧_ = 0–10, we find that more compact discs form more massive and denser clumps. The maximum clump mass increases from ∼ 10[5] to ∼ 10[7] M⊙, and the fraction of clumps exceeding the surface density of 300 M⊙⊙ pc[[−][2]][[2]] rises from 0 _._ 25 to 0 _._ 38 between _𝑧_ = 0 and 10 in 10[10] M⊙ haloes. Star formation becomes correspondingly bursty, and the global star formation efficiency after three disc rotations increases from 5 × 10[−][3] to 2 × 10[−][1] in 10[[10]] M⊙⊙ haloes and from 2 × 10 × 10 10[[−][2]][[2]] to 4 × 10 × 10 10[[−][1]][[1]] in 10[[11]] M⊙⊙ haloes as the redshift increases from _𝑧_ = 0 to 10. The accompanying feedback disrupts the gas discs of the most compact systems, while prominent stellar spiral arms emerge. Self-gravitationally bound star clusters form only in compact discs. We find no bound star clusters at _𝑧_ ≤ 2 in 10[10] M⊙ haloes, whereas the bound cluster mass fraction reaches ≈ ≈ 40 per cent at _𝑧_ ≥ 8 and ≈ ≈ 70 per cent in the most compact 10[11] M⊙ halo.

We have investigated how the compactness of galactic discs regulates clumpy star formation and the formation of bound star clusters. To this end, we have developed a new star formation model (CSF) in which star-forming gas clumps are identified on-the-fly and converted into stars with an efficiency _𝜖_ SF set by the clump surface density Σc, calibrated against the radiation hydrodynamics simulations of Fukushima & Yajima (2021). We apply the model to isolated disc galaxies embedded in haloes of _𝑀_ h = 10[9] , 10[10] and 10[11] M⊙ with a fixed gas-to-halo mass ratio of 0 _._ 01, adopting disc scale radii 

appropriate for _𝑧_ = 0–10 as a proxy for compactness. Our main results are summarised as follows. 

(i) Compact discs form more massive and denser gas clumps. In the 10[10] M⊙ haloes, the maximum clump mass increases from ∼ 10[5] _[.]_[1] to 10[7] _[.]_[4] M⊙ and the maximum clump surface density from ∼ 10[2] _[.]_[9] to _>_ 10[4] _[.]_[0] M⊙ pc[−][2] between _𝑧_ = 0 and 10. The fraction of clumps exceeding Σc _,_ th = 300 M⊙ pc[−][2] rises from 0 _._ 25 at _𝑧_ = 0 to 0 _._ 34 at _𝑧_ = 6 and 0 _._ 38 at _𝑧_ = 10, and the most compact discs host clumps with _𝜖_ SF ∼ 1.

The maximum clump mass increases surface density of 300 M⊙⊙ pc[[−][2]][[2]] rises from 0 _._ 25 to 0 _._ 38 10[[10]] M⊙⊙ haloes and from 2 × 10 × 10 10[[−][2]][[2]] to 4 × 10 × 10 10[[−][1]][[1]] in 10[[11]] M⊙⊙ feedback disrupts the gas discs of the most compact systems, cluster mass fraction reaches ≈ ≈ 40 per cent at _𝑧_ ≥ 8 and ≈ ≈ broadly consistent with those inferred for high- _𝑧_ **Key words: 1 INTRODUCTION** How galaxies convert gas into stars on the scale of individual clouds remains one of the central unsolved problems in galaxy formation. Stars form within giant molecular clouds (GMCs), which are clumpy and dense structures embedded in the interstellar medium (ISM), and the efficiency of this conversion is regulated by the interplay between self-gravity and stellar feedback. Once massive stars are born, stellar feedback processes such as photoionisation, radiation pressure, and supernova (SN) explosions inject energy, momentum, and metals into the surrounding ISM, dispersing their parent GMCs (e.g. Kruijssen et al. 2019; Chevance et al. 2022; Schinnerer & Leroy 2024; Härer et al. 2025; Wainer et al. 2026). The dispersed gas subsequently cools, re-condenses, and forms new GMCs, where the next generation of stars emerges (e.g. Inutsuka et al. 2015). This continuous gas–star cycle regulates the evolution of galaxies from the early Universe to the present day. Understanding how gas within GMCs is converted into stars is therefore essential for revealing the physical mechanisms that drive galaxy formation and evolution.

(vi) Among the runs that form bound clusters, the bound cluster mass fractions at _𝑡_ = 3 _𝑡_ dyn range from ≈ 10 to ≈ 70 per cent, consistent with the cluster mass fractions inferred for observed high- _𝑧_ clumpy galaxies, and the stellar masses of our 10[10] and 10[11] M⊙ haloes overlap the observed sample. Our model thus offers a viable route to forming such systems, although it does not reach the most extreme fractions of ≳ 80 per cent reported for the Misty Moons (Nakane et al. 2025). 

We emphasise that these simulations are idealised since the discs are isolated and non-cosmological, the halo-to-disc mass ratio is fixed, and no stellar disc is included in the initial conditions. Thus, environmental effects, gas accretion, and hierarchical growth are absent by construction. The controlled setup adopted here allows the effects of compactness to be isolated, and the next step is to test the same physics in a cosmological context, where disc sizes, gas accretion and merger histories are set self-consistently rather than as free parameters. We will carry out such simulations with the CSF model in the near future.

(v) The choice of star formation prescription is itself a leading factor. In the 10[10] M⊙ haloes, the KS runs retain their gas discs at all redshifts, show no strongly bursty histories, reach peak SFRs an order of magnitude below the CSF runs at _𝑧_ = 10, and saturate at SFE ≈ 5 × 10[−][2] for _𝑧_ ≥ 6 instead of continuing to rise with compactness. The resulting global SFEs are lower than in the CSF runs by factors of a few.

(ii) This shift in clump properties translates directly into more efficient and burstier galactic star formation. In the 10[10] M⊙ haloes, the global SFE at _𝑡_ = 3 _𝑡_ dyn increases monotonically from 5 × 10[−][3] at _𝑧_ = 0 to 2 × 10[−][1] at _𝑧_ = 10, with peak SFRs of ∼ 1 M⊙ yr[−][1] reached before _𝑡_ ≈ _𝑡_ dyn for _𝑧_ ≥ 6. Less compact discs instead form stars intermittently at 10[−][2] –10[−][1] M⊙ yr[−][1] . 

(iii) The accompanying feedback disrupts the gaseous discs of the most compact systems. The _𝑧_ ≥ 8 galaxies retain little gas near the centre by _𝑡_ = 3 _𝑡_ dyn, whereas the _𝑧_ ≤ 2 discs survive three rotations. Stellar spiral arms show the opposite trend, becoming progressively more prominent towards higher _𝑧_ , indicating that compact discs assemble dynamically coherent stellar structures on timescales of ∼ 100 Myr even while their gas is being expelled.

In all simulations, we find gas clumps with high star formation efficiencies of _𝜖_ SF ≳ 0 _._ 1, originating from compact clumps with Σc ≥ Σc _,_ th. In particular, the _𝑧_ = 6, 8, and 10 simulations produce clumps with extremely high efficiencies of ∼ 1. ## _3.1.3 Bound star clusters_ 

We here present the results for the formed star clusters, with particular focus on self-gravitationally bound systems. However, due to the effect of gravitational softening, compact star clusters formed from highly efficient gas clumps may artificially disperse, even though such clusters are expected to remain compact (Fukushima & Yajima 2021). Therefore, we define self-gravitationally bound star clusters as those formed in gas clumps with a star formation efficiency of _𝜖_ SF ≥ 0 _._ 3, rather than using the ratio of kinetic to potential energy. The value corresponds to the gas surface density of Σc ≳ 1 _._ 3 × 10[3] M⊙ pc[−][2] . This choice is motivated by the fact that star clusters formed in clouds with such high efficiencies are expected to remain self-gravitationally bound (Baumgardt & Kroupa 2007). 

The top panel of Fig. 5 shows the time evolution of the fraction of the total mass in self-gravitationally bound star clusters, _𝑀★,_[bound] c , relative to the total stellar mass, _𝑀★_ . We find that this fraction strongly depends on galactic compactness. In the _𝑧_ = 0 and 2 simulations, no self-gravitationally bound clusters form throughout the entire simulation time, indicating that star clusters in these systems originate from relatively diffuse gas clumps. In contrast, the _𝑧_ = 4, 6, 8, and 10 simulations do form self-gravitationally bound star clusters. At _𝑡_ ≈ _𝑡_ dyn, the bound cluster mass fractions in these higher- _𝑧_ simulations reach ∼ 10 %. The global star formation efficiency at t = 3 t_dyn increases from approximately 5 × 10^-3 (0.005) at z=0 to approximately 2 × 10^-1 (0.2) at z=10 in 10^10 M⊙ haloes.
